newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs seen reversing opposition to presidency.
newsitem.headline: Serbs seen reversing opposition to presidency.

text.p: The Serb member of Bosnia's post-war presidency is showing signs of reversing his opposition to cooperating with the three-man body elected last month, a senior international official said on Thursday.
Assembled foreign dignitaries were embarrassed when Momcilo Krajisnik stayed away from last Saturday's inaugural meeting in Sarajevo of the collective presidency, citing security fears.

Colum Murphy, spokesman for Carl Bildt, the international community's High Representative in Bosnia, said the Serbs had now indicated they might be ready to attend a presidency meeting in Sarajevo, the city they besieged for 43 months.
"The Bosnian Serbs painted themselves into a corner on Saturday. Now they are painting themselves out of a corner," Murphy said.
Krajisnik had earlier suggested a meeting could be held in Pale, the Bosnian Serbs' mountain stronghold near the capital.
"But now we recieve a variety of signals that Pale wishes to cooperate and move ahead with the work of the new presidency," Murphy told a news conference.
"That is to be welcomed but we still need to see these positive signals that are coming from Pale through various people crystalised into action."

Murphy said the Serbs had indicated they were ready to reverse their opposition to signing the loyalty declaration that Moslem and Croat deputies had already subscribed to following the first post-war elections on September 14.
Some opposition parties complained that an unannounced change in the way seats were allocated had worked to their disadvantage and benefited the nationalist parties.

David Foley, spokesman for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the body charged with supervising the elections, acknowledged that the formula had been changed without any announcement "in the rush of events".
This had been done because the originally published method of seat allocation had been found to be unworkable.
The OSCE apologised for the change, which meant that two parties did not receive a seat they might otherwise have had, but Foley added: "The final results are not subject to change."
Foley said local elections next month would now be held on November 23 and 24. He declined to say why polling was being held on two days instead of three, as announced earlier.
He also declined to comment on suggestions that the Bosnian Serbs would not cooperate with the OSCE over the elections.

Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic was quoted by the Belgrade-based VIP news service as telling the head of the OSCE mission in Bosnia, Robert Frowick, that the Serbs would call elections and set the rules themselves.
Frowick has been reported as carrying out a series of crisis meetings with the Serb leadership over the elections, but Foley declined comment on the issue.
Murphy said only: "There has been a regrettable pilgrimage of people to Pale."
Frowick and U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum were scheduled to meet Plavsic in Banja Luka on Friday.
